BMI was a significant independent factor for arterial stiffness in young prehypertensive subjects.
BMI is significantly correlated with arterial stiffness and found to be the independent contributing factor in the prehyptensive stage.
arterial stiffness is more pronounced in the prehypetensive stage itself and is more pronounced in individuals who have higher BMI.

the early detection of arterial stiffness and its association with higher BMI and prehypertension.

the impact of BMI on arterial stiffness in young prehypertensive individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
obesity and hypertension are the two sides of the same coin and should be treated as a single entity.
obesity and prehypertension are associated with increased arterial stiffness and the combination of these two conditions is more deleterious.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BMI is an independent risk factor for arterial stiffness in prehypertension.
the BMI is an independent factor for the development of vascular damage in the prehypetensive stage.
the prehypertensiveness with higher BMI is a risk factor for early vascular damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMI can be used as a marker for arterial stiffness in prehypertension.
the prehypertensivity with higher BMI can be considered as a risk factor for the development of arterial stiffness and cardiovascular disease in the long term.
arterial stiffness can be used as an early predictor of cardiovascular risk in young prehypertensive population.
